blocks.x: I was born in 1887, the 31st day of July, right here in Algiers.
Did any of your family play instruments, your daddy or anybody?
Yes, I had a, my father played a guitar and my brother, he's two brothers, they're both musicians too, you know.
What was your daddy's name?

Paul, Paul. Who did he play with, Peter? Well he played, he used to have a band, Old Man Dorset they call it years ago, they had, he didn't use over three or four pieces then, you know, violin, trumpet and guitar and bass, violin, you know. And how about your brothers, what were their names? Henry, he's a bass player, he's in Oakland. And Charlie, he's a banjo player, you know. He's downtown then, over in the city, you know.
Yeah. How old were you when you started taking an interest in music?
Well, right out of school. I started learning about, I was about 13 years old. And when I was about seven, 18, I was playing professionally, you know.
Did you just sort of pick it up, you know.

No, no, I was taught, you know. Taught? Who was your teacher? A professor from, I came here from France, you know, he was with the opera, he came, that day, those days, they had the French opera, you know. Yeah. And all those musicians would come from France, you know, and some of them would stay here, you see. And then they would teach, you know.
Do you remember what this guy's name was?

His name was 49 was his first name. You don't remember his second name? No, I can't remember his second name. What sort of things did he teach you, you know. Well, violin, music, violin. I taught, he taught me the violin, see. That's how I started on the violin, you know. Then I picked up trumpet later on, you know.
Yeah. How old were you when you went to these lessons, you remember?
About 13, 14 years.
How long did you go to him for lessons? About three years. Oh, just on violin? Yeah. I took the trumpet later, you know. He was playing, was he, with the French opera there?
Yeah, he was a violin playing with the French opera. You know, the French opera went down in 1918, you know.
Yeah, yeah.
I was playing a long time before that, you know.
Yeah, sure. Yeah. How about your two brothers? Did they start playing after you or before you? After me, yeah. After you. Uh-huh. What was the first band you started playing with?

Well, the first band I started was, let's see, the Superior, I think, was the first band. And then I played with Papa Celestine, you know, different fellows. Remember who was in the Superior? Well, that's Bunk, you know, his fellow here, Bunk Johnson and Billy Marrera, and Louis Nelson, myself, Buddy Johnson.
Uh-huh.
And Walter Brunney was playing drums, you know. Oh, yeah. Yeah. That's the same as that photo, that photograph with them on? Yes, that's the one. Yeah.
What uniforms did they have? You know, what color were their uniforms? Well, they were blue. Uh-huh. That's the blue. Dark blue, like that?
Yeah, dark blue, yeah. Uh-huh.
Uh-huh. What kind of stuff did you play with that band?

Well, we played mostly stocks, you know, in this old job, the music, we played a lot of that too, you see. But those days we used to get those stock numbers, you know. Yeah. All right, stock arrangements, you see.
Uh-huh. Did you all read music in that band?
Oh, yes, yes.
Even the drummer?
Uh-huh.
And would you play the lead on the violin?
Yes, uh-huh.
Uh-huh. How long were you in that band?

Oh, I stayed with them a good while. Up until about, you see, 1915 I think, when Pierre and I got together. And we started playing together, you know, and then we played, clean up until the 30s we played together. It was about, oh, about 15 years we were together with that one. Mm-hmm .
The New Trumpet Knows The New Trumpet Knows The New Trumpet Knows
Just like the one you've got on your trumpet knows?
Yeah, I got one that, I got that when I was up in Boston. That's the straight new thing. Oh yeah, you went up to Boston? Yeah. With Bishy. And they got them big cup mules, you know.
Yeah. How did you get that job up in Boston with Bishy?

Well, he sat down and asked me when I come, you know. I had my sister living in Mount Vernon, see. So I was working in insurance then, so I said well, I'll go up there and stay a little while, and see my sister, all at the same time and come back home, you see. I never intended to stay away, you understand, but I remember when I got up there, George, George Foster, you know, he was playing bass. So he said to me, Pete, when we go back to New York, you're going to stay with me? I said yeah. Man, I was thinking about staying in New York and nowhere else. What kind of jobs did you play up there?
You play in one place at the time?
Nightclub. Nightclub.
Yeah. That was with Sidney by Cheyenne? Yeah.

That was the bar club. There was nothing to it. You weren't playing nothing. You were playing little head tunes and screeching summertime, you know, on a sopranos sax. There was nothing to it. You get on the stand and play 15 minutes like that and get off, you know? Yeah. There was no dancing or nothing. No dancing? Only piano, trumpets, drums, and sopranos sax.
Remember who the pianofile was?
Yeah, from up in New York called George Trump. George Trump.

Remember the drummer? Yeah. Put it off a minute. Peter Pocosch, 6th of February 1962, tape 3. I guess you're about one of the oldest playing musicians around, trumpet players. Can you remember any of the old time guys like Buddy Bolden and Whitman? Oh yeah.

I remember Buddy. I was quite young though. He died young too. He was an old fellow when he died. He must have been in his thirties, you know? What kind of trumpet playing did you make? Well he was mostly a blues player, you know? Mostly blues. He mostly make tunes, you know, like a pallet on the floor or blues and things like that. That's mostly the type of band they had, you know? Well he'd play jobs, you know? He'd play jobs, you know.

No, I mean would he play a job, you know? He'd play a job, you know? No, I mean would he play trumpet all the time when they were playing that number or would he let down and let the other instruments solo?

Oh yeah. All trumpet players are going to take down some, you know, but he can't stay up all the time. Oh yeah. All trumpet players are going to take down some, you know, but he can't stay up all the time. Do you remember who was in Buddy's band when you saw him? the bass palette on the floor, the blues and things like that. That's mostly the type band they had, you know.
Would he play all the time? Well he'd play a job, you know. No, I mean would he play trumpet all the time when they were playing that number, or would he let down and let the other instruments solo?
Oh yeah, all trumpet players are going to take down some units, he can't step all the time.
Do you remember who was in Buddy's band when you saw him?

I might remember a few of those fellas. I think he was Buddy, and the Runs of Stores, Bob Lyons, Cornish was playing trombone. I think Brock Mumford was playing, yes, Brock Mumford was playing guitar, and a fella called Frank Lewis was a clarinet player. And I think Jamesy Phillips up here played the drums. You see when Bowling went crazy, you know, he's the Hart and Jackson. Well Frankie Dewson took the band then. The same fellas that Bowling had, Frankie took them over and called it the Eagle Band, see. He was a trombone player, see. Well instead of Bowling, he had a fella called Edward Clem, an old trumpet player. He was a figure too, you know, head man. Well then I played violin with them, with Eagle Band, see. What kind of prizes did you see Buddy playing then? Well playing these balls, you know. Playing the ball. He didn't play nothing but dances once in a while, like the old Masonic Hall, or maybe we used to have lawn parties those days, you know, open air dances, you know. And that's mostly what they would play, you know.
Was he a loud trumpet player? Yeah, oh yeah, he was loud.
That was his biggest asset, you know. That was his biggest asset he had was blowing, you know, he could blow.
Did he have a big tongue?
Yeah, he was pretty good. He had a pretty fat tongue and everything, yeah. But the only thing, he didn't know what he was doing, you know, he just picked it up, you know.
Did Buddy know what key he was playing?

Well I don't know, because you see those fellas they mostly play, you know, maybe B flat, or maybe E flat, or maybe one sharp, and that's the limit, you see. But when you get around three or four flats or three or four sharps, well then they're out, you see, you see. So you just can see, well, most everything they played was in B flat or F or something like that, you know.
Did they play a lot of blues down there?
Yeah, oh yeah, that was it. Stand by them blues and everything. Slow blues? Tied on the flow blues and… Did they play them very slow? Yeah, they used to call it slow drag those days, you know.
Did they play many fast numbers?
No, not those, they didn't play nothing too fast, just a medium tempo, you know.
Do you remember Manuel Perez? Oh yeah. What kind of stuff did he play?
He was good musician. Good musician. Good reader, you know. He was loud too, you know. He liked to blow loud.
He played a sweeter tone than Bradley, I guess, did he?

Well, he had a little bit of tone, yeah, because he was taught, you know. He was a good teacher, you know. After he knew the fundamentals, you know, up to the horn, you know. Do you remember Joe Oliver? Well Joe come up, just like those other fellas, you know, starting out like that. I remember when I first saw him, I was playing with that Eagle band then. And we was playing on Rampart Street one night, just the trombones and the violin and the guitar and bass. So he came in this place with his horn, you know, that's the first time I saw him, first time Dukes and I saw him too. So he asked us to let him play, you know. So he played with us, you know, and made it all right with tunes that he knew, you know. And from then on Dukes was to hire him now and then, and to play with the band, you know. And eventually he started playing around in Storyville, you know, and playing with the brass band, playing with fellas like Perez and them, well they'd help him, you see. He would kind of coach him and he would learn a lot for free, you know. He was free schooling, you know.
Do you remember much about Freda Cuppert? I remember about Freda.

He was a, first he started on the violin, see, picking, you know. And then he picked up the trumpet, see. Well he was a loud trumpet player too. Well he played good too, you know what I'm saying? But he wasn't much in reading, you know, but he could play, you know what I'm saying? He had kind of a gift, you know what I'm saying? Something like Bechet, you know, gifted, you know.
Who were the better trumpet players around that time? Huh?

Who were the better trumpet players? Well, Perez and Kimball and a fella by name of Matoyer and those old men like Old Man and Morett, and fellas like that, you know, they were about the best men you could rely on, you know, if you hired them, if you had music, you could play, you see.
Were they old reading men?
Oh yeah. Oh yeah. Sight readers, yeah.
Remember Hippolyte Charles?

Yeah, I played with him too. He was a personal friend of mine, he was a nice fellow too. He played nice trumpet too. He was a legit trumpet, no jazz or nothing, he was straight. And there was another fellow who played nice too, Peter LaCasse. He was a legit trumpet player too.
What's the difference between a legit trumpet player and a...

Well, some men can improvise and some men play strictly about music, you see. Now you'll take some fellows, if you ain't got the parts there, they can't play, you see. They can't remember, you know. They can't commit anything to memory. And another guy will play a tune once, or play a spark once, and he don't need it the most. Well that's the difference, you see. But when you say a legit man is a man that, and if you've got music he'll play it, but he ain't going to put nothing to it, you see. He'll play it all right. But another guy will play it and then improvise on it too, you see. Build it up. Could they improvise these fellows? Well that's a gift mostly, I think. That's mostly a gift, you see. Everybody don't hear that, you know. You don't learn that. It's got to be natural, you see.
And these fellows like Twy and Black Charles, could they improvise?
Not very much. They didn't play the style we're playing now, you see. They played mostly straight, nice trumpet but straight, you know.
You could improvise? Huh? You could improvise? Oh yeah, sure.

I always could do that, you know. Well I used to play in our band. I'd play a stock two, three times, I didn't need the music anymore. I could just remember it, you understand? Sure. Just like anything else, you understand. Natural.
Do you remember any other good trumpet men around that time? No.

Particular good? Well George McCullum, he was a very nice trumpet man too. You ever read in May? Yes, very good. He taught a little Alcorn, you know, Alvin. Alvin? That's his teacher, yeah. I think they were cousins. I don't know whether they were related or not, but I know he taught him. He's very good. He played a lot in the Excelsior Band, you know.
Was Bunk a legit musician, or was he a ...

Bunk could read pretty good, you understand? He could do pretty good. He played all that job in music with us, you know. He was very good. He could improvise too, I guess. Yes, yes. He had a gift for it too. He put a lot of little extra touches, you know. Dr. Lloyd too, well he's gifted to that, you see. Like you'd be a person who'd be singing, you know. And he'd play like an obligato, you understand, in between the singing and the voice and the lead. It's really pretty, you know.
Who would you say had the best tone around, if any of the guys? Best tone? Yeah.
Well I think Mituai was, as far as tone, you know. He played more on the style of a soloist, you know. He was a nice triple-tongued man and everything, you know.
Who taught you to play trumpet, Peter?

Well the old man Brookhoven, he had a band, he was an old German, you know. And the Brookhoven band, Brass Band, you know. He had a couple of boys play trumpet and one played in the theater, you know. Leo I think his name was, but his daddy, well you see I was a musician already because I was playing violin, but all I wanted to learn was the horn. See I knew the music and everything, see. So I went to him and in a couple of lessons I had the horn down, you see, that was all the lesson. I just wanted to learn the fingering, you know.
Who taught you to play trombone? Hmm? Who taught you to play trombone? Trombone? Myself.

Yeah. Or xylophone and then band. Yeah, let's pick that up. Let's pick it up. Well the xylophone is similar to the piano, you see. If you know the chords on the piano, you can come in there playing the xylophone, because it's just like a piano keyboard, you know. But the trombone, I just took it and I knew the bass cleft and everything, you see. All I get, I learned the positions on the horn and that was all, you see. See, it's just like the violin, it's got seven positions, you know.
Do you remember any of the trumpet players like Buddy Petit and Chris Kelly?

Yeah, Chris Kelly, Buddy Petit, Rene, now he would have made a nice trumpet player that boy, if he hadn't got the proper schooling, you know. He was better than Buddy Petit. Rene, he was very good. But he was too much of a musician, but he could play the horn nice, you know, like Louis, you know. Had a nice time? Yeah, a nice, very nice time. What kind of jobs did he play? Nothing but dances, you know, like we played. Maybe one of the little nightclubs, you know. During the war he played down at the, what's the name of that place? Brown Dood? Down there, right at the Industrial Canal on St. Claude Street, right opposite the jail. We played that ten months in the place, too. Oh, I can't think of the name. Not the Brown Derby? No. You know, you know, we're at the Industrial Canal where the jail is on this side of the street. Right opposite is this club, you know, a brick front.
Not Larchens? No, no. Oh, no, that's on Almanaster. I can't think of that one.
Yeah, as far as I know that place, I can't call the name.
Well, never mind. How about Buddy Petit? What kind of stuff did Buddy Petit do? He was a head, you know, routine, very nice of him.
He used to drink a lot, though. You know what I mean?
Did they ever go in for any high notes, any of these kinds?

Well, they didn't use too many high notes them days, you know. They put most of them in the register, you know. They just started that high note business recently, you know. Most of them was the first player. Maybe once in a while they'd get up to see, you know, like that. By Chris Cully.
By Chris Cully. Hmm? By Chris Cully.

Well, Chris was a blues player, yeah. He used to play blues, man. He didn't play anything but blues much, then? No, mostly, yeah. He was up there, I guess, Sam Morgan and the fellas, you know, that's his style, you know. Remember that Sam Morgan band?
Huh? You remember the Sam Morgan band? Oh yeah, sure. He was way under me, you understand.

I was playing a long time before they were coming. All the fellas come to little country towns around, you know, like over and the fellas, they come right up the river there, you know. And they come here and start playing. Baby Dots and Johnny Dots and all of them, they come right from Louisiana. And the Kid Punch. Yeah, he's from here too, right up the country there.
Did he have any distinctive style of playing?

Well, blues, you know, blues style. He used to do some fast fingering on us. He used to do some other boy too, but he died in Chicago there. Lee Collins, well he was right from here too. They started right around here.
Tell me, in all these bands, like the Pierron band and things like that, did they ever have drum solos? Hmm? Did they ever have drum solos in any of these bands?

No, we didn't use that style. They were just, you know, straight to the good jet playing, you know, playing. Mostly rhythms, you know. They didn't use all this feature and stuff like we use now, you know.
When was the first time they started using featuring?
Well, yeah, just recently, say about ten, twelve years ago they started that, yeah. When these clubs and things started, you know, they started using the band as a show, as dance music, you know.
Tell me, Black Happy used to play drum solos down at the Lyric Theatre.
No, no, not Black Happy. There was another club. Oh, Red Happy. Red Happy, yeah. He played the, yeah. He played drum solos down there?
Well yeah, in the theatre jet they used that, you know. They had another boy came here from Texas.

He used to juggle the sticks, you know, and all that sort of stuff, you know. Eccentric, you know. Well in the show pit, you know, in the theatre pit they'd do those things, but not dance work, you know.
Did you ever play in the theatre? Yeah.
Yeah. We used to play the show, the Smart Set show. Smart Set show. Smart Set show. Smart Set, yeah.
What band was that?

That's a traveling musical show used to come out of New York, you know. And they'd come here and we'd play the show. Every time they'd come we'd play. They'd carry their own directors, you see, the piano player, you know.
What band was that then? Huh?
What band was that?
Piran. Did you ever play with any of these traveling circuses or anything? Circus?
Yeah. No, no. I never wanted to travel.
I don't know how Bunk used to play and all that.

At one time I had a, before I was married, when I was young, I had a mind to go on the road, you know, because I could have went, because I could double, you see, I could play violin and trumpet, you know. But I got married and that killed all of that, you see. That settled that too.
Yeah. When did you first meet Steve Lewis?

Well Steve, he used to go on, he traveled with a show called Billy Mack, you know. And we had another boy playing with us called Arthur Campbell. Well Arthur left me, he went to Chicago, see. Well Steve came in town and he come out and started playing with us. Well in Carroll family. Yeah, he stayed with us, yeah. But he used to travel with Billy Mack's show to play these theaters, you know, circuits, like the Lyric and there was different places, you know, around Chicago and Cleveland and things like that to play them little shows, you know.
Who taught Steve to play? Steve?
I don't know who taught Steve. No, not Steve, Steve.
Steve Lewis. He taught himself. Did he?

Yeah, he taught himself. He used good piano players, yeah. Couldn't read though, you know. Couldn't read, Steve Lewis. He had a wonderful ear, you know, gifted, you know. If we played a stock, well we had all good men, you know. And we played down once, he had it, you know. He knew all the chords and everything, you see.
How did you meet Lewis Cattrall?
Well Lewis was a baby when I was playing with his daddy.
I mean the old man. The old man? Yeah, how did you meet him? Well, that's true.

He's much older than me, you know. Just true playing in the Pierron band. You see, Bill used to play drums with us, you know, Pierron. Bill, what was that? Bill, Matthews, the trombone player? Uh huh. So when Bill left, I don't know why he left, but anyway, I made Pierron get the old man, see, because he was the style drummer we needed in that band, see.
Who taught him to play? Who?
The old man. I told you, a fellow at the theater, yeah. That's right. Yeah. Called Dusty, fine drummer, show man, you know.
What kind of stuff did he play in the Pierron band, Cattrall? Lewis Cattrall. What kind of stuff did he play? Four four rhythms? No, he was strictly, he played by music, you know. Strict by music?

Yeah. And he had a nice touch, you know, he could roll his, roll that snare drum, just perfect, you know. He was wonderful. He never used to use much cymbal playing, though. No, not those days, no. Or wood blocks, did he use much of them? Yeah, he used wood blocks. Tom-toms, did he use any of that?
Not very much. He had them, they didn't do it, by the way too much.
But he was the only one had a folding based drum.
You ever seen one like that? No, I heard about it.
Lewis, young Lewis, he told me about that. It folded up and went into a little case, well, it wasn't much bigger than that.
Yeah?
Mm-hmm. It was only photographs of that. It was made out of aluminum, you know. Yeah. That's not the one in that flange. That wasn't very much. Not very much.
It had them.
It didn't do it, but it wasn't too much. But he was the only one who had a folding based drum. You ever seen one like that? No, I heard about it.
Lewis, young Lewis. Yeah.
He told me about that. It folded up and went into a little case. Well, wasn't much bigger than that.
Yeah?
Mm-hmm.
It was only photographs of that. Do you remember?
That was pretty thin. It was made out of aluminum, you know.
That's not the one in that photograph, that folding drum, that's not the same
one as in that photograph. No, no, that's a different drum.
You've never seen a photograph of him flying on that folding drum?

It would fold like a, look like a pointy on each end like that, you know. Come around and the case was made that way. And the heads would fold up to and they'd all go right down in that little case. And it wasn't much bigger than that when he'd be traveling with it.
He used to use that with a carol band. Yeah, sure. We had it when we went to New York. He had the folding drum?
Yeah.
So he had that on the records too?

Wonderful drum band, I think. Well, in those days, you see, the drums wouldn't record, they didn't use drums. Oh, no. No. The only thing that would record in those days was the cymbal. You couldn't hear a drum or a bass drum like you can now. No, it's funny.
So on those records he had just the cymbal on the wood band?
Just the cymbal on the wood blocks. Just the cymbal on the wood blocks. Or a block, yeah. Yeah. The bass drum, snare drum wouldn't record. I couldn't understand that. Oh, I didn't see.
They got it now, right?
They record now. Yeah.
Pick up everything now. Yeah.
They can pick up if you stamp your foot? Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Well, I guess that's a better word question. You got any quick questions, Richie?
Well, do you remember a trumpet player, or a corner player called Joe Johnson, do you know? No, I don't remember a trumpet player. Or Chick Chambers, or?
Chick Chambers, yes. I remember him, yes.
What sort of trumpet player was he? He was all right. He was a head man to him. Sugar Johnny, was he the same?
Sugar Johnny, yes. Yes, I remember him too. He died in Chicago too. I don't remember if Chick's living up there yet, but he was up there. He gave up when he went up there.
Yeah. Yeah, he played around there quite a bit.
He went up Chicago around 19, 18 or 15, around then. Tell me he had a red bean place up there selling food, you know.
Another thing I meant to ask you Peter, what part does the violin play at ragtime? Do you understand what I mean?
Ragtime?
Yeah, what part does the violin play?
Well, it plays the lead, you know. It just plays the lead and improvise, you know.
It improvises, you know.
Yeah. Yeah, the violin, the lead sheet, you know. Play the melody, you know.
Yeah. Is that it? Well, there's still some more tape, and there's nothing Peter or not.
Yeah, you see that's Bill there. You see that's when Bill was playing with us, you see? Yeah. But after Bill left, then old Mike Cottrell came in, see? Mm-hmm.
That's you on that trombone.
Bill had a brother play drum, too. He used to play with us. Oh, there's none. Oh, Bebe.
Yeah, Bebe.

It's a superior band, yeah. Yeah, I'm playing trombone there. Who's that guy? Willie Edwards, his name was. That's Steve there. That's Steve there. That's Warnock. That's Warnock, if you're wrong. Oh, uh-huh.
So...
Look at this. That's you there. Yeah. That's the one in California, my brother. Henry? That's the bass player, yes. He's bass there.
Yeah, that's Henry, huh?
Yeah. That's Lloyd Warnock, too. That's Newman's daddy, see? Dwight Newman. That's Martin, and that's Charlie, see? Mm-hmm.
That's a... He looks awful young, this, this Henry Martin. Looks awful young there, doesn't he?
Yeah, Martin. Looks very young. We was playing, uh... That is the old man, Henry Martin. He never had no daddy that played drums. No.
Did he have a son, Henry Martin, that played drums?
Yeah, he had a... He had a son, but he didn't play anything.
Uh-huh.
Uh, we was playing, uh, on Bourbon Street, at the dream room, and, uh, what a dream room is, and I was a silver slipper then.
Uh-huh. But this is at the Absinthe House?
Yeah, that's what it's.
It's a photograph, yeah.

And, uh, we was playing a broadcast, remote control, and he took six. Yeah? Just in the... Yeah, we started the broadcast, you know, and he took, like, a convulsion, like, you know? Oh, uh-huh. And, uh, man, it took two minutes to hold him. I don't know what caused that, man. He was...
Was he out after that, or did he pass?
Well, he got a little bit, but he didn't last too long. Uh-huh. That wasn't good choice.
No, no, no, no.
He wasn't that big, you know? No.
Did you both play the song there?

No, but I'll switch it off now. Uh, you know those ragtime records you made with Charlie Love? Yeah. Was that the part you were playing on the violin there, was that the same sort of stuff as you play with the superior? Yeah. The same lead.
That's that Joplin music, yeah.
Yeah. Uh-huh. Yeah.
Yeah. All in... Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm .

segments.title: Birth in Algiers and musical family
segments.summary: Bocage gives his birthdate and says his father Paul played guitar in a small band; brothers Henry (bass) and Charlie (banjo) were also musicians.

segments.title: Violin lessons from a French opera teacher
segments.summary: He started at about 13 learning violin from a teacher from the French opera, for about three years, and took up trumpet later.

segments.title: First bands: Superior Band, Celestine, and the Piron partnership
segments.summary: He names the Superior Band's members and uniforms, the stock arrangements they read, and says he left around 1915 to team up with Piron for some 15 years.

segments.title: Playing a Boston and New York nightclub job with Bechet
segments.summary: He shows a trumpet mute got in Boston and describes going up to visit his sister and joining Bechet's small nightclub group with George Foster.

segments.title: Buddy Bolden: his playing, his band and the Eagle Band
segments.summary: Bocage recalls Bolden as a loud blues player, lists his sidemen, says Duson took over the band as the Eagle Band, and describes their keys and tempos.

segments.title: Manuel Perez, Joe Oliver and Freddie Keppard
segments.summary: He describes Perez as a good reader, recalls first meeting Oliver at Rampart Street, and calls Keppard a gifted but non-reading player.

segments.title: Reading trumpeters versus improvisers
segments.summary: He names the dependable reading trumpeters, explains legit versus improvising players and says improvising is a natural gift.

segments.title: Bunk Johnson's reading and who had the best tone
segments.summary: Bunk could read and improvise with extra touches; he gives his pick for best tone.

segments.title: Learning trumpet, trombone and xylophone
segments.summary: He learned trumpet fingering in a couple of lessons from Brookhoven, and taught himself trombone and xylophone.

segments.title: Chris Kelly, Buddy Petit, Rene and other trumpet players
segments.summary: He discusses Kelly, Petit and Rene, high notes, the Sam Morgan band and players who came from country towns.

segments.title: Drum solos and featuring in early bands
segments.summary: The Piron-era bands did not feature drum solos; showy drumming belonged to theatre pits and featuring began in recent years.

segments.title: Playing the Smart Set show; never traveling
segments.summary: The band played for the traveling Smart Set show, but he never wanted to go on the road after marrying.

segments.title: Steve Lewis joins the band
segments.summary: Steve Lewis traveled with Billy Mack's show before joining Bocage's band, was self-taught, could not read but had a wonderful ear.

segments.title: Lewis Cottrell Sr. replaces Bill Matthews in the Piron band
segments.summary: Bocage had Piron hire the elder Cottrell as drummer when Bill Matthews left; he describes his strict, music-reading style.

segments.title: Cottrell's folding bass drum
segments.summary: Bocage describes the aluminum folding bass drum that Cottrell carried and used with the band.

segments.title: Why drums did not record in the early days
segments.summary: Early recordings only picked up cymbal and wood blocks, not snare or bass drum.

segments.title: Chick Chambers and Sugar Johnny
segments.summary: Richie asks about Chambers and Sugar Johnny; Bocage recalls both moved to Chicago.

segments.title: The violin's role in ragtime
segments.summary: The violin plays the lead and improvises on the melody.

segments.title: Identifying musicians in a band photograph
segments.summary: Looking at a photograph, they identify Bill Matthews, Cottrell, Steve Lewis, Henry and Charlie Bocage, Henry Martin and others.

segments.title: A bandmate's seizure during a radio broadcast
segments.summary: Bocage tells of a bandmate who had a convulsion during a remote broadcast at a Bourbon Street club.

segments.title: Ragtime records with Charlie Love
segments.summary: The violin lead on the ragtime records is the same as played with the Superior Band, Joplin music.
